title: Rockefeller's University Rises
voiceover: Before the gray Gothic towers, before the gargoyles and the quiet courtyards, there was a different University of Chicago. It opened in the 1850s, and it stood about two and a half miles north of where the campus sits today, near 35th Street and Cottage Grove Avenue. The land came from Stephen A. Douglas, the United States senator from Illinois. Douglas first offered the tract to the Presbyterians, on the condition that they raise a hundred thousand dollars for a building. They couldn't. So he gave the ten acres to a group of Baptists instead, and the school was chartered in 1857, with Douglas himself as the first president of its board of trustees. That school never had enough money. The financial panic of 1857 wiped out most of the early pledges almost as soon as it opened. Douglas died in 1861, and his name was a problem for fundraisers. He had written the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the law that let new territories vote slavery in, and many donors in the North wanted nothing to do with anything attached to him. The trustees built anyway, past what they could afford. They put up a five-story main building of stone and kept enrolling students even as the bills came due. The debt climbed for thirty years. There was a fire. In 1886 the creditors foreclosed, the classes stopped, and the first University of Chicago was finished. It had run for nearly three decades and never escaped the hole it started in. So when people say the University of Chicago was founded in 1890, they mean the second one. It was a clean break. At its last meeting, the old board renamed itself the Old University of Chicago, on purpose, so the new Baptist school could take the name with no legal strings attached. There would be no shared debt, no shared trustees, no shared anything. The new institution wanted a fresh start, and it had the money to buy one. That money came from one man. In 1889, John D. Rockefeller pledged six hundred thousand dollars toward a new university in Chicago. By that point his Standard Oil controlled around ninety percent of the oil refining in the United States. He was, by most measures, the richest man in the country. He was also a devout Baptist, and the Baptists had wanted a great university in the Midwest for years, a flagship to match the older eastern schools. But Rockefeller did not simply write a check. He attached a condition. Other donors had to come up with four hundred thousand more before his money was good. It was a dare as much as a gift. The American Baptist Education Society went out and raised the four hundred thousand. With the match in hand, the University of Chicago incorporated in 1890. Marshall Field, who owned the great department store on State Street, gave the first ten acres of land in Hyde Park, six miles south of downtown, fronting the Midway Plaisance between two parks that Frederick Law Olmsted had laid out. The campus would rise on the blocks from 57th to 59th Street, between Ellis and Woodlawn. To run it, Rockefeller and the trustees chose William Rainey Harper. Harper was thirty-five. He had earned a doctorate from Yale at nineteen, in Semitic languages, and he taught Hebrew with a kind of fame that was unusual for a scholar. He was a Baptist, ambitious, and in a hurry. He stayed in a hurry his whole life. He drove himself without rest, and he died in office in 1906, of cancer, at forty-nine, fifteen years into the job. He and his wife are buried in the chapel on the campus he built. And he had a model in mind. A generation earlier, Johns Hopkins had opened in Baltimore as the first true research university in the country, built on the German idea that a university should not just teach old books but produce new knowledge. Harper wanted that for Chicago, and he wanted it bigger. He did not want a quiet college. He wanted graduate study and laboratories, a university press, and a faculty of stars, and he wanted it all at once, on day one. He built things into the place that were strange for the time. The university was coeducational from the start, admitting women alongside men. He split the calendar into four quarters and kept the doors open year round, so a student could enroll in summer and graduate whenever the work was done. He started the University of Chicago Press, which began publishing scholarly books and journals in 1892 and is still running. He built an extension division to carry university classes out to working adults across the city. To fill the faculty, Harper used Rockefeller's money the way few presidents could. He offered salaries no one else could match and went hunting. The most famous raid was on Clark University, in Worcester, Massachusetts. Harper came away with something like two-thirds of its faculty and half of its graduate students. The president of Clark never forgave him. When the first classes opened on October 1, 1892, the University of Chicago already had a faculty of around a hundred and twenty, eight of them former college presidents, and an enrollment of 594 men and women. A university that had not existed three years earlier opened its doors fully formed. One of Harper's early hires tells you what kind of place he was building. He brought in Amos Alonzo Stagg to run physical culture and coach football, and he gave Stagg a salary of twenty-five hundred dollars and a tenured professorship. A football coach, on the regular faculty, with tenure. That was nearly unheard of, and it set a pattern other universities would follow for decades. The campus itself was designed by a Chicago architect named Henry Ives Cobb. Cobb laid out a plan of six connected quadrangles and designed eighteen of the early buildings, all in English Gothic Revival, all faced in gray Bedford limestone from Indiana. The first building finished was Cobb Hall, ready for that opening day in 1892, and it held the classrooms and offices the young university needed all at once. Because Cobb worked from a single master plan, the buildings that came after his, raised by other architects over the following decades, kept to the same gray limestone and the same Gothic line, so the campus reads as one piece even though it went up over many years. Cobb modeled the campus on Oxford and Cambridge, the courtyards and the narrow passages and the long sight lines, the crenellations and the gargoyles and the grotesques carved into the stone. It was new construction made to look six hundred years old. Chicago was barely sixty years old as a city. The University of Chicago, two years old, was already dressing itself in the costume of an ancient one. And the timing was almost theatrical. As the first buildings went up, the World's Columbian Exposition was being built right next door, in Jackson Park and along the Midway Plaisance, the southern edge of the campus. The fair opened in 1893, a temporary city of white plaster palaces and the first Ferris wheel, drawing millions of visitors past the new university's gates. The exposition came down within the year. The limestone quadrangles stayed. Rockefeller kept giving. In the university's first decade he put in about thirty-five million dollars, an enormous sum for the time. He later called it the best investment he ever made, and he meant it as money well spent. The institution that money built did not stay inside its gates. From the start, it shaped the neighborhood around it, who could buy there, who could rent there, who could live near the quads at all. The years after the First World War were the years of the Great Migration. Hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners came north to Chicago looking for work and for distance from Jim Crow. The city packed most of them into a narrow corridor on the South Side that people called the Black Belt, where the housing was scarce and the rents were high. By the 1920s, Black families were pressing outward from that corridor, and many of them were heading toward Woodlawn, just across the Midway from campus. In 1928, the Woodlawn Property Owners Association organized a racially restrictive covenant in the northwest part of Woodlawn, a legal agreement among white owners not to sell or rent to Black buyers. The university backed it, quietly, with lawyers and money. From 1933 to 1947, the University of Chicago spent more than a hundred and ten thousand dollars on what it called community interests. More than eighty-three thousand of that went to defending and enforcing restrictive covenants in Hyde Park, Washington Park, and Woodlawn. Many of the restricted properties belonged to the university itself. It tried to keep its name off the covenants in public, but the connection was no secret. In 1937, an editorial in the Chicago Defender, the city's great Black newspaper, called those agreements the University of Chicago Agreement to get rid of Negroes. The president through these years was Robert Maynard Hutchins, who led the university from 1929. The Black attorney Earl B. Dickerson, one of the law school's first Black graduates, went to Hutchins with two other lawyers and asked him to stop the university from backing the covenants. By their account, Hutchins answered that he could not allow Black residents near the university because it would hurt enrollment. Then in 1948, the United States Supreme Court ruled in Shelley versus Kraemer that courts could no longer enforce racial covenants. The agreements stayed in the property records, but they lost their teeth. So the same dollars that raised the limestone towers, the same institution that hired the stars and carved the gargoyles, also paid lawyers to keep a line drawn around the campus. The Gothic quads looked like Oxford. The thing they were protecting was something much closer to home. That word, protected, the one people used for Hyde Park's parks and its lake and its university, would carry that second meaning for a long time to come. The towers are still here. The carved stone is still here. And so is the question the carving was meant to answer, namely who the neighborhood was built for, and who it was built to keep out.
